# Podcast Prep Outline — "AI in Banking"
**Hosts:** David O'Hara & Ryan Suchala | **Format:** The Improving Edge | **Runtime:** ~30 min | **Audience:** Fintech professionals, banking executives, business leaders

## Episode Overview
Banking sits on the most regulated, highest-quality data of any industry, and that should be an AI advantage, not a liability. Instead, most banks are stuck between two extremes: the largest players (JPMorgan, Goldman, Bank of America) are running hundreds of production AI use cases, while regional and community banks remain in pilot purgatory, throttled by legacy cores, data quality gaps, and a regulatory environment that just got a lot more explicit. This episode traces that arc: why banking's data advantage is real, why it's so hard to unlock, what the new rules demand, and what separates the banks pulling ahead from the ones falling behind.

---

## Topic 1: The Regulated Data Advantage Nobody's Using
**Summary:** Banks hold decades of clean, structured, regulated data (KYC, transaction history, credit files) that fintechs would kill for, but most treat it as a compliance burden instead of a strategic asset.
**Grounding:** JPMorgan runs 400+ production AI use cases on an enterprise ML platform processing ~$10T in daily transactions, built on top of years of data plumbing investment before agent deployment.
**Question for Ryan:** "Everyone assumes fintechs have the data edge because they're 'AI-native.' Why is that backwards, and what does a bank actually have that a fintech doesn't?"
**Narrative purpose:** Opens with the counterintuitive hook. Sets up the whole episode's thesis: the advantage exists, but almost nobody is capturing it.

## Topic 2: The Trillion-Dollar Head Start
**Summary:** The largest banks aren't just ahead, they're compounding: JPMorgan directs $2B of an $18B tech budget to AI with $1.5B in cumulative savings; Bank of America has 300+ approved use cases across 200,000 employees.
**Grounding:** JPMorgan's COIN program reviews 1.2M hours of legal work annually; Bank of America allocates $4B of a $13B tech budget to AI.
**Question for Ryan:** "When a bank can spend $4 billion a year just on AI, what does that actually buy them that a mid-size regional bank structurally cannot replicate?"
**Narrative purpose:** Establishes the scale gap early so the audience understands what "winning" looks like before we get into why most banks aren't there.

## Topic 3: The Data Quality Wall
**Summary:** Before any bank can act on its regulated data advantage, it has to survive its own data quality problem, which is the single biggest reason AI projects stall.
**Grounding:** More than 90% of bank data users report needed data is unavailable or too slow to retrieve; nearly a third of bankers cite data quality or accessibility as their top AI adoption obstacle.
**Question for Ryan:** "If the data advantage is real, why are a third of bankers saying data quality is what's actually stopping them?"
**Narrative purpose:** First reality-check. Moves from advantage to obstacle, starting the "implementation reality" phase of the arc.

## Topic 4: Legacy Cores, The Silent Killer
**Summary:** Most large banks run on core systems dating to the 1990s or earlier, and bolting AI onto a COBOL-based core is expensive, slow, and often the real reason "pilot mode" never ends.
**Grounding:** Deloitte's 2026 Banking & Capital Markets Outlook names fragmented data foundations and outdated legacy systems as primary throttles on AI adoption industry-wide.
**Question for Ryan:** "Walk us through what it actually looks like, technically, to try to connect a modern AI model to a core banking platform that's older than some of the engineers building the model."
**Narrative purpose:** Grounds the abstract "legacy systems" complaint in something concrete listeners can picture, deepening the implementation-reality section.

## Topic 5: SR 26-2, the Rules Just Changed
**Summary:** In April 2026, the Fed, OCC, and FDIC jointly issued SR 26-2, the biggest update to model risk management guidance since SR 11-7 in 2011, and it now requires continuous drift monitoring, not periodic checkbox validation.
**Grounding:** SR 26-2 supersedes SR 11-7, mandates tiered model inventories by materiality, and requires real-time tracking of performance drift, data drift, and algorithmic bias.
**Question for Ryan:** "For folks who aren't compliance nerds, what actually changed with SR 26-2, and why does it matter that regulators moved from 'check the model once a year' to 'watch it continuously'?"
**Narrative purpose:** Pivots the episode into the regulatory/compliance core, the meatiest and most differentiated section for a banking-exec audience.

## Topic 6: The Generative AI Gray Zone
**Summary:** SR 26-2 explicitly carves out generative and agentic AI as too novel to formally regulate yet, which sounds like a free pass but is actually the riskiest position a bank can be in.
**Grounding:** SR 26-2 excludes gen AI/agentic AI from formal scope; regulators and the OCC have both signaled that existing risk management practices should still apply even without a formal rule, and formal RFIs on AI model risk are already in motion.
**Question for Ryan:** "If regulators haven't written the rule yet, does that mean banks get to move faster with generative AI, or does it mean they're more exposed if something goes wrong?"
**Narrative purpose:** Introduces tension and stakes. This is the "risk" beat the audience is here for, and it's genuinely unresolved, which makes for good conversation.

## Topic 7: Protecting the Golden Source
**Summary:** As generative AI and synthetic data start touching core repositories, banks face a new integrity risk: contaminated data that's realistic enough to be undetectable, pushing institutions toward locked-down "golden source" vaults and retrieval-augmented approaches.
**Grounding:** M&T Bank uses retrieval-augmented generation to limit generative AI to internal, governed data specifically to control this risk; industry analysts flag 2026 as the year synthetic data contamination becomes a real operational threat.
**Question for Ryan:** "Explain the golden source vault idea to someone who's never heard of it. Why can't banks just let AI models learn from everything they've got?"
**Narrative purpose:** Gives a concrete, technical mitigation the audience can act on, balancing the risk beat with a solution.

## Topic 8: Explainability and the Human Accountability Line
**Summary:** Regulators keep coming back to the same core worry: AI decisions that touch customers need to be explainable, auditable, and ultimately traceable to a human who's accountable, which is much harder with generative and agentic systems than with traditional scoring models.
**Grounding:** The Federal Reserve and OCC have both flagged lack of explainability, data poisoning, and validation gaps as open governance challenges; GAO's 2025 report on AI in financial services echoes the same concerns.
**Question for Ryan:** "Where's the line for you, at what point does a bank need a human to actually own an AI-driven decision, versus letting the system run on its own?"
**Narrative purpose:** Closes the compliance/risk block on the most human, most debatable question, transitioning naturally toward "who's winning."

## Topic 9: The Widening Gap Between Leaders and Laggards
**Summary:** Fintechs built AI into their operations from day one and are deploying at scale, while many traditional banks are still stuck in proof-of-concept mode, and the gap is starting to show up in M&A activity focused on plugging AI and data capability gaps.
**Grounding:** Deloitte's 2026 outlook contrasts fintechs "deploying at scale" against banks "stuck in pilot mode"; industry analysis shows M&A shifting from scale-for-scale's-sake to targeted acquisitions of AI, data, and niche capabilities, with bank charters themselves becoming a strategic tool.
**Question for Ryan:** "If you're advising a regional bank that knows it's behind, is the answer to build, to buy, or to partner? What actually closes that gap fastest?"
**Narrative purpose:** Sets up the competitive dynamics question directly, moving the episode from problem-space into strategy and action.

## Topic 10: What Autonomous Finance Actually Looks Like
**Summary:** The leading edge, Goldman Sachs co-developing autonomous agents for trade reconciliation and compliance, points to where this all goes: agentic systems handling real financial workflows end to end, and the banks that get governance right now will be the ones trusted to deploy it first.
**Grounding:** Goldman Sachs has 12,000 engineers paired with AI agents and is co-developing autonomous agents for accounting, compliance, and client onboarding; its GS AI Assistant is now firmwide across the organization.
**Question for Ryan:** "Paint the picture five years out. What does 'autonomous finance' actually mean for a customer, and who gets to build it first, the big banks or the fintechs?"
**Narrative purpose:** Closing beat. Answers the "future state" promise from the open and gives listeners a clear, memorable takeaway on what separates winners from laggards, the governance and data discipline built up over the whole episode, not just raw AI adoption.

---

## Timing Note
10 topics x 3 minutes each = 30 minutes. Topics 1-2 (advantage/scale) run faster and more energetic; topics 5-8 (regulatory core) are the densest and may need the tightest moderation to stay in-window; topics 9-10 close on strategy and vision to end high-energy.
